claim: CLC secondary active transporters exchange Cl- for H+.
source: CLC secondary active transporters exchange Cl- for H+.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CLC transporters supported by extensive literature and is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Crystal structures have suggested that the conformational change from occluded to outward-facing states involves only the rotation of a conserved glutamate (Gluex) upon its protonation.
source: Crystal structures have suggested that the conformational change from occluded to outward-facing states is unusually simple, involving only the rotation of a conserved glutamate (Gluex) upon its protonation.
evidence: This claim is based on prior crystallographic studies cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: As [H+] is increased to protonate Gluex and enrich the outward-facing state, a residue ~20 Å away from Gluex, near the subunit interface (Y419), moves from buried to solvent-exposed.
source: Using 19F NMR, we show that as [H+] is increased to protonate Gluex and enrich the outward-facing state, a residue ~20 Å away from Gluex, near the subunit interface, moves from buried to solvent-exposed.
evidence: This claim is supported by 19F NMR experiments showing TEMPOL accessibility changes at Y419 as a function of pH (Figures 3B-D).

claim: Inter-subunit cross-linking at D417C reduces transport activity.
source: Consistent with functional relevance of this motion, constriction via inter-subunit cross-linking reduces transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing decreased Cl- transport with increasing cross-linking (Figure 4D).

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that the D417C cross-link dampens extracellular gate-opening motions.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that the cross-link dampens extracellular gate-opening motions.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulations showing reduced collective motions that open the extracellular gate in cross-linked D417C (Figure 8C).

claim: Mutations that decrease steric contact between Helix N and Helix P (F357A and L361A) remove the inhibitory effect of the D417C cross-link.
source: In support of this model, mutations that decrease steric contact between Helix N (part of the extracellular gate) and Helix P (at the subunit interface) remove the inhibitory effect of the cross-link.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing that F357A and L361A mutants are insensitive to D417C cross-linking (Figure 11D).

claim: CLC transporters catalyze the exchange of Cl- for H+ with a strict stoichiometry of 2 Cl- for every H+.
source: From bacteria to humans, Cl-/H+ exchange by CLC transporters occurs with a strict stoichiometry of 2 Cl- for every H+ (Accardi and Miller, 2004; Picollo and Pusch, 2005; Scheel et al., 2005; Jayaram et al., 2011; Leisle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies demonstrating the 2:1 stoichiometry.

claim: CLC transporters must follow an alternating access mechanism to achieve stoichiometric exchange.
source: To achieve this stoichiometric exchange, CLCs must follow an alternating access mechanism, in which bound substrate ions access either side of the membrane alternately, i.e., they cannot access both sides simultaneously (Patlak, 1957; Jardetzky, 1966; Shilton, 2015).
evidence: This is based on established principles of transporter function cited in the manuscript.

claim: In all other active transporters that have been structurally or biophysically characterized, the conformational changes governing interconversion between major functional states involve significant protein motions.
source: In all other active transporters that have been structurally (or biophysically) characterized, the conformational changes governing the interconversion between these major functional states involve significant protein motions, including reorientation of helices or even entire domains (Shi, 2013; Paulino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature comparing CLC transporters to other transporter families.

claim: CLC transporters are homodimers in which each subunit independently catalyzes Cl-/H+ antiport.
source: CLC transporters are homodimers in which each subunit independently catalyzes Cl-/H+ antiport (exchange) (Robertson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural and functional studies.

claim: The central anion-binding site (Scen) is stabilized by a positive electrostatic potential created by the N-termini of Helices F and N as well as by interactions with conserved Ser and Tyr residues.
source: The central anion-binding site (Scen) is stabilized by a positive electrostatic potential created by the N-termini of Helices F and N as well as by interactions with conserved Ser and Tyr residues, which physically occlude the anion from the intracellular side (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural information shown in Figure 1A and established knowledge of the CLC structure.

claim: The conserved Tyr contributes to an intracellular gate that opens to generate an inward-facing state.
source: Using cross-linking as an alternative approach to crystallography, Basilio et al. demonstrated that the conserved Tyr contributes to an intracellular "gate" that opens to generate an inward-facing state (Basilio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited cross-linking studies by Basilio et al.

claim: Movement of Helix O is required in conjunction with movement of the Tyr-gate residue for generating the inward-facing state.
source: While this inward-facing state has not yet been structurally characterized in detail, the elegantly designed cross-linking studies demonstrated that movement of neighboring Helix O (Figure 1B) is required in conjunction with movement of the Tyr-gate residue.
evidence: This is based on cited cross-linking studies demonstrating coupled movements.

claim: In the E148Q mutant structure, the Gln side chain swings upwards and the site previously occupied by the side chain is occupied by an anion.
source: In the structure of a mutant in which Gln is used as a proxy for the protonated Gluex, the side chain swings upwards and the site previously occupied by the side chain is occupied by an anion (Figure 1C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of E148Q shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the E148Q structure, the pathway to the extracellular solution is very narrow – too narrow to accommodate Cl- or other permeant ions.
source: However, in this structure the pathway to the extracellular solution is very narrow – too narrow to accommodate Cl- or other permeant ions (Miloshevsky et al., 2010; Krivobokova et al., 2012) – suggesting that additional conformational changes are required for the formation of the OF state in order for external anions to access the external anion-binding site (Sext).
evidence: This is based on computational analyses of the E148Q structure cited in the manuscript.

claim: The pKa of Gluex is ~6.
source: Since the pKa of Gluex is ~6 (Picollo et al., 2012), a change in pH from 7.5 to 5.0 will cause Gluex to transition from mostly deprotonated to mostly protonated, and therefore from its position occupying Sext outward towards the extracellular solution.
evidence: This is based on cited experimental measurements of the Gluex pKa.

claim: Crystallization at pH 4.6 failed to reveal any conformational change in CLC transporters.
source: Although crystallization at pH 4.6 failed to reveal any conformational change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Dutzler et al., 2002), spectroscopic approaches have shown that H+-dependent changes do occur outside the restraints of crystallization.
evidence: This is based on cited crystallographic studies and comparison with spectroscopic data.

claim: Helix R undergoes H+-dependent conformational change during the transport cycle.
source: Using environmentally sensitive fluorescent labels, Mindell and coworkers showed that Helix R, which lines the intracellular vestibule to the Cl--permeation pathway (Figure 1B), undergoes H+-dependent conformational change during the transport cycle (Bell et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited fluorescence studies by Mindell and coworkers.

claim: H+-dependent structural change occurs at Helix R and at the linker connecting Helices P and Q.
source: Using site-specific NMR labeling schemes, our lab has identified H+-dependent structural change at Helix R and also at the linker connecting Helices P and Q (P/Q linker) (Figure 1B) – a region ~20 Å distant from the Cl--permeation pathway (Elvington et al., 2009; Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior NMR studies from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Y445 and Y419 were identified as undergoing H+-dependent changes in chemical shift in BuriedOnly ClC-ec1.
source: Of the five buried Tyr residues in ClC-ec1, two reported [H+]-dependent changes in chemical environment. The first, as expected, was at Y445, which is within 6 Å of Gluex; the second, strikingly, was in a region ~20 Å away, at Y419 near the dimer interface (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on 19F NMR data from the BuriedOnly construct (Figure 2B).

claim: The Y419only mutant shows robust, fully coupled Cl-/H+ exchange activity.
source: Although the "Y445only" mutant was unstable and could not be further examined, the "Y419only" mutant (Figure 3A) was stable and showed robust, fully coupled Cl-/H+ exchange activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing Cl- and H+ transport with proper stoichiometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Y445F mutant exhibits wild-type behavior.
source: The functionality of the Y419only mutant may seem startling, given that it involves mutating the highly conserved Cl--coordinating Tyr445 (Figure 1C) to Phe, but it is consistent with previous structural and functional studies demonstrating wild-type behavior of the Y445F mutant (Accardi et al., 2006; Walden et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on cited studies showing that Y445F retains function.

claim: The 19F NMR spectrum of Y419only at pH 7.5 shows a single 19F peak centered at -60 ppm.
source: The 19F NMR spectrum of Y419 only at pH 7.5 shows a single 19F peak centered at 60 ppm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR spectrum shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Y419 19F peak shifts upfield and splits into two peaks when [H+] is increased.
source: This peak shifts upfield and splits into two peaks when [H+] is increased, indicating that the 19F nucleus has experienced a change in chemical environment.
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR spectra shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At pH 7.5, there is little sensitivity of the 19F-Y419 signal to 100 mM TEMPOL.
source: At pH 7.5, there is little sensitivity of the 19F-Y419 signal to 100 mM TEMPOL (Figure 3C) which is consistent with the largely buried position of Y419 in the crystallographically captured state of ClC-ec1, i.e., 12–13 Å from the protein surface (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectra showing minimal line-broadening at pH 7.5 (Figure 3C).

claim: At pH 4.5, significant line-broadening of the Y419 19F signal is observed in the presence of TEMPOL.
source: In contrast, at pH 4.5, significant line-broadening is observed (Figure 3C), indicating exposure of Y419 to the bulk solution allowing a close approach, or direct contact, of the TEMPOL probe with the fluorine atom (Esposito et al., 1992; Niccolai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectra showing substantial line-broadening at pH 4.5 (Figure 3C).

claim: The H+-dependent change in Y419 accessibility is reversible.
source: This H+-dependent change in accessibility is reversible, as demonstrated by the reappearance of the Y419 signal when pH is returned to 7.5 from 4.5 in the presence of 100 mM TEMPOL (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectra showing signal recovery upon pH reversal (Figure 3D).

claim: In channel-like ClC-ec1, Y419only exhibits a single NMR peak at ~-61 ppm that is sensitive to line-broadening by TEMPOL at both pH 4.5 and 7.5.
source: In this channel-like background, Y419only exhibits a single NMR peak at ~-61 ppm, and this signal is sensitive to line-broadening by TEMPOL at both pH 4.5 and 7.5 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectra showing TEMPOL sensitivity at both pH values (Figure 3E).

claim: The crystal structure of channel-like ClC-ec1 variant E148A/Y445A superposes closely with WT (RMSD 0.52 Å).
source: The accessibility at pH 7.5 is surprising given that the crystal structure of channel-like ClC-ec1 variant E148A/Y445A superposes closely with WT (RMSD 0.52 Å) and indicates a buried position for Y419 (Jayaram et al., 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Y419C forms spontaneous inter-subunit cross-links.
source: We found that Y419C forms spontaneous inter-subunit cross-links and, to our surprise, that these cross-links have no detectable effect on function (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE showing dimer formation and flux assays showing no effect on activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: D417C forms spontaneous inter-subunit disulfide cross-links, with ~50% of the protein migrating as a dimer on non-reducing SDS-PAGE.
source: Like Y419C, D417C forms spontaneous inter-subunit disulfide cross-links, with ~50% of the protein migrating as a dimer on non-reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 4C, top panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cross-linking at D417C correlates directly with a decrease in transport activity.
source: These assays show that cross-linking at 417C correlates directly with a decrease in transport activity (Figure 4D), with Cl- and H+ transport inhibited in parallel (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing decreased activity with increasing cross-linking (Figure 4D).

claim: Immediately after purification and before CuP treatment, essentially all of the 417C residues in channel-like ClC-ec1 are available as free thiols.
source: Immediately after purification and before CuP treatment, essentially all of the 417C residues are available as free thiols (Figure 4E, bottom panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by thiol quantification assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Lowering the pH from 7.5 to 4.5 induces a shift in the D417C-D417C distance distribution from a peak shorter than 20 Å to a peak at 20 Å.
source: At pH 7.5, the distribution is dominated by a single peak at a distance shorter than 20 Å (Figure 4G). Lowering the pH to 4.5 induces a shift to a peak at 20 Å (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DEER distance distributions shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The channel-like D417C-MTSSL exhibits an altered distance distribution profile compared to the WT background.
source: The channel-like D417C-MTSSL exhibits an altered distance distribution profile compared to the WT background (Figure 4H), suggesting that the protein adopts a different conformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DEER distance distributions shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The D417C-D417C distance in channel-like is increased relative to that observed in the WT background at pH 7.5.
source: Notably, the D417C-D417C distance in channel-like is increased relative to that observed in the WT background at pH 7.5 (Figure 4I), consistent with the resistance of the channel-like protein to cross-linking (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of DEER distance distributions shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The cross-linked D417C backbone superposes on WT ClC-ec1 with a Cα RMSD of 0.57 Å.
source: Our crystal structure, determined at 3.15 Å resolution, reveals a backbone that superimposes on WT ClC-ec1 with a Cα RMSD of 0.57 Å (Figure 5A, Table 2).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of cross-linked D417C determined in this study (Figure 5A, Table 2).

claim: Extra density connecting the 417C residues confirms the formation of an inter-subunit disulfide bridge in the crystal structure.
source: Extra density connecting the 417C residues confirms the formation of an inter-subunit disulfide bridge (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron density maps shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both in the absence and presence of cross-link, D417C binds Cl- robustly, with an affinity somewhat stronger than observed with WT (Kd ~0.1–0.2 mM vs 0.6 mM).
source: Both in the absence and presence of cross-link, D417C binds Cl- robustly, with an affinity somewhat stronger than observed with WT (Kd ~0.1–0.2 mM vs 0.6 mM) (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: D417C in the E148A mutant background is readily cross-linked by CuP.
source: In contrast to D417C/channel-like ClC-ec1, we found that D417C in the E148A mutant background is readily cross-linked by CuP (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cross-linking of D417C/E148A is associated with significant inhibition of activity.
source: Nevertheless, cross-linking of D417C/E148A is associated with significant inhibition of activity (Figure 6B, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing decreased activity with cross-linking (Figure 6B).

claim: The double mutant D417C/Y445S transports Cl- at ~850 s-1 and H+ at ~20 s-1 yielding a Cl-/H+ stoichiometry of ~43.
source: The double mutant D417C/Y445S transports Cl- at ~850 s-1 (Figure 6C) and H+ at ~20 s-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) yielding a Cl-/H+ stoichiometry of ~43, similar to that of the Y445S single mutant (Walden et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays measuring Cl- and H+ transport (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cross-linking of D417C/Y445S proceeds to ~70% and inhibits Cl- transport by ~60%.
source: Cross-linking of D417C/Y445S proceeds to ~70% and inhibits Cl- transport by ~60% (Figure 6D), with extrapolation to 100% cross-linking yielding a turnover of ~0 (± 100 s-1) (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays and cross-linking analysis (Figure 6D, Table 1).

claim: The D417C cross-link has no effect on water entry into the hydrophobic region between Gluin and Gluex.
source: In contrast to the A404L mutation, which greatly reduces water permeation through the portal (Han et al., 2014), the D417C cross-link has no effect on water entry (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations showing similar water entry in WT and cross-linked D417C (Figure 7B).

claim: The cross-link at residue 417 dampens the opening of the extracellular gate in WT ClC-ec1.
source: A search over the 20 dominant collective motions obtained through the PCA of the entire WT MD simulation revealed that deformations along some of the collective motions increase the distances between these pairs by >1.5 Å and thus are coupled to gate opening. To conduct a statistical analysis of these motions, we divided the entire simulation trajectory into six blocks and determined the number of times such collective motions occur in each block (Figure 8C, blue bars). An identical analysis performed on the MD simulation trajectory obtained from the cross-linked D417C mutant revealed that the motions that open the extracellular gate are dampened due to the cross-linking (P=0.002 – 0.008) (Figure 8C, orange bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations and principal component analysis (Figure 8C).

claim: The cross-link at residue 417 does not significantly dampen the distance changes around the intracellular gate.
source: Unlike the extracellular gate, however, the cross-link at residue 417 does not significantly dampen the distance changes around the intracellular gate (P=0.338) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations and principal component analysis (Figure 8D).

claim: The radius profile of the ClC-ec1 Cl- transport tunnel shows an extracellular bottleneck with a minimum radius of ~0.2 Å.
source: The radius profile of the ClC-ec1 Cl- transport tunnel, calculated using the program HOLE (Smart et al., 1996), shows an extracellular bottleneck with a minimum radius of ~0.2 Å (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structure using the HOLE program (Figure 9).

claim: The calculated radius profile for both the E148A mutant and the channel-like variant E148A/Y445A reveal extracellular bottlenecks with minimum radii of ~0.9 Å.
source: Interestingly, the calculated radius profile for both the E148A mutant (lacking Gluex) and the channel-like variant E148A/Y445A also reveal extracellular bottlenecks. (E148A/Y445A was evaluated rather than the E148A/Y445S construct used here because this is the only channel-like variant for which there is a crystal structure.) With minimum radii of ~0.9 Å (Figure 9) these bottlenecks are still too narrow to allow Cl- permeation (r(Cl-) ≈ 1.81 Å) (Shannon, 1976).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of crystal structures using the HOLE program (Figure 9).

claim: There are fewer collective motions that can open the extracellular gate in cross-linked channel-like ClC-ec1 compared to uncross-linked channel-like.
source: The analysis revealed that there are fewer collective motions that can open the extracellular gate after the cross-link is introduced to the channel-like mutant (P=0.001–0.070) (Figure 10A), whereas the intracellular gate was not significantly affected (P=0.354) (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations and principal component analysis (Figure 10A,B).

claim: Helix N makes direct contacts to Helix P through side-chain packing of conserved residues in each Helix.
source: Visual inspection reveals an obvious potential transduction pathway: Helix N, which forms part of the extracellular gate (Figure 1B, Figure 8A), makes direct contacts to Helix P through side-chain packing of conserved residues in each Helix (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 11A,B.

claim: The D417C cross-link only weakly inhibits L361A activity and completely fails to inhibit F357A.
source: Strikingly, the D417C cross-link only weakly inhibits L361A activity and completely fails to inhibit F357A (Figure 11C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing minimal or no effect of cross-linking on these mutants (Figure 11D).

claim: The activity of the A404L mutant is reduced further by the D417C cross-link despite being similarly sluggish to F357A.
source: We found that the activity of the A404L mutant, despite being similarly sluggish to F357A, is reduced further yet by the D417C cross-link (Figure 11E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing inhibition of A404L by cross-linking (Figure 11F).

claim: The structure of the E148Q mutant represents an 'outward-facing occluded' state.
source: Our results describe a previously unidentified protein conformational state and suggest a new framework for understanding the CLC transport mechanism, introducing two key concepts. First, the structure of the E148Q mutant, with the side chain rotated away from Sext (Figure 1C) represents an "outward-facing occluded" (OFoccluded) state (Stein and Litman, 2014), in which bound Cl- does not have full access to the extracellular solution.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and the narrow pathway observed in the E148Q structure.

claim: H+ binding promotes an 'outward-facing open' state involving conformational rearrangement of Helices N and P that widens the extracellular ion-permeation pathway.
source: Second, H+ binding promotes an "outward-facing open" (OFopen) state, involving conformational rearrangement of Helices N and P (Figure 11A), that widens the extracellular ion-permeation pathway in comparison to the known crystal structures.
evidence: This is based on NMR, cross-linking, DEER, and MD simulation data showing conformational changes at Helices N and P.

claim: Helix N motions have been strongly implicated in the mammalian antiporter CLC-4.
source: In support of this idea, we note that Helix N motions have been strongly implicated not only in ClC-ec1 (the results presented here) but also in the mammalian antiporter CLC-4 (Osteen and Mindell, 2008).
evidence: This is based on cited studies on CLC-4.

claim: Cross-linking of Y419C, just 5 Å away from D417C, does not inhibit function.
source: First, the cross-linking of Y419C, just 5 Å away from D417C, does not inhibit function (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flux assays showing no effect of Y419C cross-linking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cross-linking does not significantly affect water entry via the narrow portal that is the rate-limiting barrier for formation of water wires and H+ transport.
source: Second, any large movement of Helix P would likely have a major effect on water entry via the narrow portal that is the rate-limiting barrier for formation of water wires and H+ transport (Lim et al., 2012; Han et al., 2014). Since our computational analysis indicates that cross-linking does not significantly affect water entry (Figure 7), Helix-P motion may involve only a small tilt or rotation that exerts a "lever-arm" effect on Helix N and the Cl--entryway.
evidence: This is based on MD simulations showing no effect of cross-linking on water entry (Figure 7B).

claim: Simultaneously cross-linking Helices I and Q, and the H-I and I-J loops had no significant effect on function.
source: Third, previous inter-subunit cross-linking studies targeting Helices I and Q, and the H-I and I-J loops showed that simultaneously cross-linking these regions had no significant effect on function (Nguitragool and Miller, 2007) and therefore argue against a major restructuring of the inter-subunit interface.
evidence: This is based on cited cross-linking studies.

claim: The rearrangements at Helices N and P are likely small in magnitude and do not involve the entire inter-subunit interface.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rearrangements at Helices N and P are likely small in magnitude and do not involve the entire inter-subunit interface.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including cross-linking studies and MD simulations.

claim: Computational studies using normal-mode and functional-mode analysis showed the subunit interface remaining largely intact even as other regions of ClC-ec1 underwent global conformational changes.
source: This conclusion is in line with computational studies using normal-mode and functional-mode analysis, which showed the subunit interface remaining largely intact even as other regions of ClC-ec1 underwent global conformational changes to alternately expose Cl-- and H+-binding sites during the exchange process (Miloshevsky et al., 2010; Krivobokova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited computational studies.

claim: Helix R has been pinpointed in experimental studies of H+-dependent conformational change.
source: One of the mobile helices identified in these computational studies was Helix R, which has also been pinpointed in experimental studies of H+-dependent conformational change (Bell et al., 2006; Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: The OFopen state lowers Cl- affinity and promotes Cl- release.
source: Second, we hypothesize that the OFopen state lowers Cl- affinity and promotes Cl- release, as suggested by the increase in Cl--binding affinity observed when formation of the OFopen state is inhibited by the D417C cross-link (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is based on ITC data showing increased Cl- affinity in cross-linked D417C (Figure 5D,E).

claim: The crystal structure of channel-like ClC-ec1 reveals a narrow constriction at the extracellular-gate region.
source: Previously, it was recognized that the narrow pathway depicted by the crystal structures of channel-like ClC-ec1 is not sufficiently wide to allow rapid ion conduction and that protein dynamics (either breathing or conformational change) must play an important part in the mechanism of ion conduction (Jayaram et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on cited structural studies of channel-like ClC-ec1.

claim: Channel-like ClC-ec1 populates a conformation different from that seen in the crystal structure and exhibiting similarities to the new OFopen state.
source: Our results clarify the issue by showing that channel-like ClC-ec1 populates a conformation different from that seen in the crystal structure and exhibiting similarities to the new OFopen state characterized in these studies.
evidence: This is based on NMR and cross-linking data showing that channel-like ClC-ec1 adopts a conformation similar to WT at low pH.

claim: Transition to the inward-facing state involves motion of the intracellular half of Helix O.
source: Using a cross-linking strategy, Basilio et al. showed that transition to the inward-facing state involves motion of the intracellular half of Helix O.
evidence: This is based on cited cross-linking studies by Basilio et al.

claim: Helix O motion is thought to be limited in scope, as it is relayed directly to the intracellular gate via a steric interaction between intracellular-gate residue Y445 and Helix O residue I402.
source: This motion is thought to be limited in scope, as it is relayed directly to the intracellular gate via a steric interaction between intracellular-gate residue Y445 (Figure 2A) and Helix O residue I402 (Basilio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited cross-linking studies.

claim: Helix O makes direct contacts to Helices N and P.
source: Nevertheless, since Helix O also makes direct contacts to Helices N and P (studied here), it seems likely that intracellular and extracellular gate-opening motions will be linked through the interaction of these three helices.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of helix contacts.
